strengths: Well-motivated and novel problem framing: repurposing pre-trained 2D flow matching priors (FLUX.1-dev) for panoramic perception (RGB→X: distance, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic) alongside generation and completion, going beyond the appearance-only focus of prior 2D-lifting scene generation methods.

PanoX fills a real gap: to the authors' knowledge it is the first panoramic dataset with dense geometry AND PBR material annotations covering both indoor and outdoor scenes, and it is thoughtfully split into Train/Val/Test plus OutDomain scenes for generalization evaluation.

Strong empirical results: consistent state-of-the-art performance on panoramic intrinsic decomposition (Table 2) with large margins (e.g., albedo PSNR 17.8 vs. 10.9 for DiffusionRenderer) and competitive geometry estimation despite using far less training data than MoGe.

Useful architecture analysis: a clear taxonomy of cross-modal adapter designs (Shared-Branch, Shared-Adapter, Separate-Adapter) with a controlled ablation (Table 4) justifying the Separate-Adapter choice, plus ablations on camera rays, joint material modeling, and joint geometry modeling that yield practically useful findings (e.g., cross-attention joint modeling of PBR materials beats channel concatenation).

Complete and convincing end-to-end demonstration: the image→panorama→multimodal panorama→mesh→PBR/relighting/physical simulation pipeline shows the practical value of graphics-ready scene generation, and limitations are candidly discussed (distance accuracy, metallic generalization, inference cost).
Unified flow-matching formulation (MIMO loss over multiple conditions/outputs) is clean, general, and applicable beyond panoramas.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to synthetic data: PanoX-OutDomain is still rendered with the same engine and asset pipeline, so 'unseen scenarios' do not test cross-engine or real-world generalization; the claims of in-the-wild generalization are supported only by qualitative figures in the supplementary, not quantitative benchmarks (e.g., no evaluation on real HDR panorama sets or standard 360 depth benchmarks).

The PanoX dataset is relatively small in scene diversity (8 large-scale scenes, 6 used for training/testing), which limits the strength of generalization claims and the long-term value of the benchmark; the authors themselves attribute poor metallic generalization to data scarcity.

The graphics-ready 3D scene generation (Sec. 3.4, Fig. 8) is demonstrated only qualitatively via demos; there is no quantitative evaluation of reconstruction quality, seam artifacts, exploration consistency, or relighting fidelity against baselines such as LayerPano3D or DreamCube.

Comparisons to geometry baselines (MoGe, DepthAnyCamera) are somewhat uneven: narrow-FoV or non-panorama-trained methods are evaluated out of their design scope, which inflates the apparent advantage; a head-to-head with a panorama-specific depth method under matched training data would be more informative.
Depth/distance accuracy remains behind MoGe (AbsRel 0.158 vs. 0.106), and the acknowledged 'bumpy' surfaces directly affect the headline application (PBR rendering quality), which is not quantified.

Reproducibility concerns: key implementation details are sparse or deferred (number of training iterations, adapter ranks, training data volume for HDR360-UHD prompts via BLIP2, seam-blending details, inference time/steps), and no code or data release is explicitly promised in the manuscript.

PBR material estimation quality relative to the 2D generative prior is questioned by the authors' own limitations section, which slightly weakens the core claim that 2D generative priors are well suited to intrinsic PBR perception.

strengths: The paper targets a clear and underexplored problem: existing panorama-based 2D lifting pipelines generate appearance but neglect intrinsic properties (PBR materials, geometry), which blocks integration into graphics pipelines. Framing perception, generation, and completion in a unified flow-matching formulation is a sensible and well-motivated design.

The cross-modal adapter study (Shared-Branch vs. Shared-Adapter vs. Separate-Adapter, Tables 4-7) is a genuine ablation-driven contribution, and the finding that separate LoRAs per input preserve pre-trained priors is useful for practitioners adapting DiT models to multi-modal tasks.

PanoX fills a real gap: to the authors' credit, no prior public panoramic dataset offers dense geometry + PBR material annotations across both indoor and outdoor scenes (Table 1). The occlusion-aware mask sampling (Fig. 5) for training completion models is a nice, practical detail.

The application pipeline (mesh from distance map, spherical UV unwrapping, PBR relighting, physical simulation in Blender) demonstrates that the outputs are actually usable in graphics workflows, which is more than most 2D-lifting papers show.
Limitations are candidly discussed (Appendix E), including bumpy reconstructed surfaces, poor metallic generalization, and doubts about whether 2D generative priors truly help PBR estimation.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is thin and largely self-referential. PanoX contains only 8 scenes, and the headline quantitative results (Tables 2-3) are computed on PanoX-OutDomain, i.e., just 2 held-out scenes. Panoramic perception claims of state-of-the-art rest on very little scene diversity; results could be scene-specific. A claim of this scope needs substantially broader evaluation (e.g., Structured3D test, MatrixCity, real panoramic captures).

Baseline comparability is questionable. Competitors such as RGB↔X, IID, IDArb, and MoGe were not designed for panoramas; DiffusionRenderer had to be fed multi-frame renderings of each panorama. Large gaps (e.g., 17.8 vs. 10.9 PSNR on albedo) plausibly reflect domain mismatch rather than architectural superiority, and the paper does not control for this (e.g., fine-tuning baselines on PanoX).

The geometry results undercut the 'graphics-ready' claim. OmniX ranks only second on distance (behind MoGe, AbsRel 0.158 vs. 0.106) and the normal Mean angular error of ~27° is far behind narrow-FoV SOTA (typically <12°). The authors themselves admit distance prediction is 'not accurate enough, resulting in bumpy reconstructed 3D surfaces.' Since the entire 3D pipeline is built on the distance map, this is a substantive weakness, not a cosmetic one.

Panoramic generation and completion are evaluated only qualitatively (Appendix B-C; no metrics, no user study, no comparison to LayerPano3D, DreamCube, or WonderWorld on this task), despite generation being one of the three claimed capabilities and a headline element of Figure 1.

Practicality concerns are acknowledged but unresolved: diffusion-based perception via FLUX.1-dev is slow for a task (depth/normal/material estimation) where discriminative models run in real time; the 12 adapter models must be trained and switched per task; and the ERP seam problem is only patched with horizontal blending rather than solved.

Reproducibility and release plans are not stated: no mention of code or PanoX public release, and the 'HDR360-UHD' dataset used for generation training is cited only via an older Text2Light paper, making the exact training data ambiguous. Text descriptions for PanoX are machine-generated (Florence-2), which raises questions about their usefulness for text-to-panorama training that are not analyzed.

The writing has notable sloppiness for a final submission: duplicated references (Raistrick 2023a/b, WonderJourney 2024c/d), a broken cross-reference ('Text2light... Chen et al., 2022' citation mismatch in Sec. 4.2), inconsistent dataset terminology (HDR360-UHD vs. Text2Light), and typos ('to constructing', 'and and'). A methodology section that claims a 'unified formulation' should also more carefully distinguish which components are new versus inherited from prior adapter/LoRA literature.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: existing panorama-based 2D-lifting methods focus on appearance generation and neglect intrinsic perception (albedo, roughness, metallic, normals), which blocks integration of generated scenes into PBR graphics pipelines. Repurposing pre-trained 2D flow matching models (FLUX.1-dev) for panoramic perception is a sensible and timely insight.

The unified formulation (Eq. 3) elegantly casts generation, perception (RGB→X), and masked completion (X→X with masks) into a single conditional flow-matching framework, and the Separate-Adapter design is a simple yet effective architectural contribution, supported by a thorough ablation (Table 4) showing clear gains over Shared-Branch and Shared-Adapter alternatives.

PanoX is a genuinely useful community resource: to the authors' knowledge it is the first panoramic dataset covering both indoor and outdoor scenes with dense geometry AND material annotations (distance, normal, albedo, roughness, metallic), addressing a real data gap (Table 1).

Strong quantitative results on panoramic intrinsic decomposition (Table 2), with large margins over strong baselines such as DiffusionRenderer and IID, and competitive geometry estimation despite using much less training data than MoGe (Table 3).

The downstream demonstrations (graphics-ready 3D scenes supporting PBR relighting, free exploration, and physical simulation) convincingly validate the practical utility of the predicted intrinsic maps, going beyond qualitative panorama quality.

Additional ablations on PBR material arrangement (Table 6), joint geometry modeling (Table 7), and camera-ray conditioning (Table 5) provide useful empirical guidance for practitioners adapting diffusion backbones to perception tasks. The limitations section is candid about slow inference, inaccurate distance prediction, and weak metallic generalization.
The paper is well written and clearly organized; the occlusion-aware mask sampling for training completion models is a thoughtful detail.
weaknesses: Evaluation is almost entirely on the authors' own synthetic benchmark (PanoX-Test / PanoX-OutDomain). Although held-out scenes are used, the ground truth comes from the same renderer/generator family as the training data, which may favor OmniX over baselines (e.g., IID, IDArb, RGB↔X) that were designed for and trained on real/narrow-FoV data. The very large gaps in Table 2 (PSNR 17.8 vs ~10) should be interpreted with this domain bias in mind; evaluation on real panoramic data (e.g., a human study or metrics on real HDR panoramas) would substantially strengthen the claims.

The PanoX dataset is built from only 8 large-scale scenes (5 indoor, 3 outdoor), which is limited in scene diversity and raises concerns about overfitting despite the held-out scenes; the paper would benefit from a discussion or quantitative measure of scene variability.

Panoramic generation is evaluated only qualitatively (Appendix B); no quantitative metrics (FID, CLIP-score, or comparison against DreamCube/LayerPano3D/others) are reported for the image-to-panorama task, so the 'generation' half of the unified claim is under-evidenced.

Despite the 'unified' framing, the system actually consists of 12 separately trained task-specific adapter models; there is no single model handling multiple modalities/tasks jointly (and Tables 6-7 show joint modeling often does not help). The unified contribution is thus mainly at the formulation level rather than the deployed model level.

Geometry estimation is second-best to MoGe (Table 3), and normal accuracy (mean ~27°, 5°-error rate 0.155) remains far from precise; the authors acknowledge that distance inaccuracies lead to bumpy 3D surfaces, which somewhat undercuts the 'graphics-ready' claim for demanding PBR use.

The ERP seam-continuity handling is borrowed from LayerPano3D rather than addressed within the proposed framework; this limitation of the DiT positional encoding is noted but not analyzed or resolved.

Reproducibility details are thin: no training duration/iteration counts, no statement of whether PanoX or model weights will be publicly released, and training on Ascend NPUs may complicate reproduction for others. Baseline evaluation protocols (whether competitors were fine-tuned on PanoX or run zero-shot) are not clearly specified.

The camera-ray conditioning ablation (Table 5) is essentially inconclusive (mixed results), yet camera rays are still presented as an optional component; a clearer recommendation or removal would tighten the story.

strengths: The core insight—repurposing pre-trained 2D flow-matching priors (Flux) for panoramic *perception* (PBR materials, geometry) rather than only appearance generation—is well-motivated and addresses a genuine gap: prior panorama-based 2D-lifting methods rely on off-the-shelf depth estimators and lack intrinsic/material outputs needed for graphics pipelines.

Circular Synchronization is an elegant, principled contribution: enforcing circular translation equivariance directly in spatial operators (circular padding + RoPE-aware circular attention with token padding and masking) is a training-free, structurally grounded alternative to latent blending, and the qualitative comparison in Fig. 10 against circular blending and latent rotation convincingly supports the claim of near-seamless generation.

The Separate-Adapter design for cross-modal conditioning is a sensible architectural contribution, and the ablation (Table 5) is informative: it isolates the benefit of modality-specific LoRAs from both adapter sharing and pre-training initialization, showing pretrained priors help even for modalities with very different pixel statistics.

PanoX is a valuable dataset contribution: the first panorama dataset spanning indoor and outdoor scenes with pixel-aligned dense geometry and PBR material annotations (Table 1 comparison supports this claim), with proper train/val/out-of-domain splits enabling generalization evaluation.

The paper reports strong, broad empirical evidence: SOTA on panorama generation against CubeDiff/Diffusion360/PanoDiffusion, large margins on intrinsic decomposition (Table 3), competitive geometry estimation with far less training data than MoGe (Table 4), panorama completion results in the appendix, and multiple design ablations (camera rays, PBR material input arrangements, joint distance-normal modeling) that honestly report negative or negligible results.

The limitations section is candid and substantive (inherited diffusion inefficiency, bumpy surfaces from imprecise distance prediction, poor metallic generalization, doubts about whether 2D priors truly benefit PBR estimation), which strengthens scientific credibility.
weaknesses: The 3D scene construction pipeline—the headline application enabling PBR-ready scenes—is evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. 11 demos in Blender). There is no quantitative assessment of reconstruction quality, relighting correctness, or downstream task utility, so the 'graphics-ready 3D scene' claim rests largely on demonstrations. The authors' own admission of bumpy surfaces suggests the end-to-end 3D quality is currently modest.

Perception evaluation fairness is a concern: OmniX is trained on PanoX and evaluated on PanoX-OutDomain, while competing methods (RGB↔X, MGNet, IID, DiffusionRenderer) were not trained on PanoX-style panoramic PBR data. The large margins in Table 3 may partly reflect training-data alignment rather than methodological superiority; a comparison under matched training data or stronger discussion of this would strengthen the claims.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art performance across both' generation benchmarks is overstated: on SUN360, FID is notably worse than CubeDiff (39.4 vs 25.5) and FAED is also worse; only KID, CLIP-FID, and CLIP Score improve. The abstract and Sec. 4.2 should be more precise.

Some quantitative tables contain suspicious or under-explained entries: in Table 4, normal Mean (27.14) vs Median (14.88) ordering is inconsistent with other rows (e.g., OmniData-v2 median 100.60 > mean), and some baselines show values (5°/30° metrics as 0.019–0.269 vs OmniX 0.155/0.663) whose units/semantics are unclear; these need clarification for the results to be fully interpretable.

PanoX derives from only 8 scenes (6 for training/validation), raising concerns about scene-level diversity and overfitting; text captions are generated automatically with Florence-2 without any quality validation, and only 512×1024 training resolution limits fine detail.

The framework requires 12 separately trained adapters (plus fine-tuned OmniX-Fill variants), which is operationally heavy and somewhat at odds with the 'unified' framing; inference inherits the slow multi-step diffusion ODE sampling, acknowledged but not quantified.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the project page URL is truncated/empty in the manuscript, and there is no explicit statement of code/data release, which matters given the dataset is a central contribution.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: extending panorama-based 2D lifting beyond appearance generation to perception of intrinsic properties (geometry, albedo, roughness, metallic), which enables graphics-ready (PBR-ready) 3D scene construction rather than view-only synthesis.

Circular synchronization is a clean, principled contribution: enforcing circular translation equivariance directly in the spatial operators (circular padding for convolutions, token padding + attention masking for RoPE attention) is training-free, preserves the pre-trained generative prior, and is a more fundamental alternative to post-hoc latent blending. The qualitative comparison in Fig. 10 is convincing.

The modality-specific (Separate) adapter design is well-ablated (Table 5), including a from-scratch control that supports the claim that 2D generative priors transfer to non-RGB modalities; the PBR material input arrangement study (Table S3) adds useful practical insight.

PanoX addresses a genuine data gap: the first panorama dataset covering both indoor and outdoor scenes with dense geometry and material annotations, with a reasonable in-domain/out-of-domain split protocol.

The experimental scope is broad: panorama generation on standard benchmarks (Laval Indoor, SUN360) against established baselines, intrinsic estimation against five recent methods, geometry estimation against six, completion against Flux-Fill, and downstream demos (relighting, simulation, free exploration).

Limitations are candidly and specifically discussed (bumpy reconstructed surfaces, poor generalization of metallic prediction, limited benefit of 2D priors for PBR material estimation), which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness concerns. For geometry estimation (Table 4), OmniX is trained on PanoX and Structured3D, whereas DepthAnywhere/DepthAnyCamera/MoGe are evaluated zero-shot on PanoX-OutDomain; the favorable comparison to MoGe (which the authors acknowledge uses 9.0M depth annotations) is thus confounded by in-domain training. Similarly, in Table 3 the Structured3D evaluation set overlaps with the training data for OmniX but not necessarily for all baselines. These comparisons overstate the advantage.

The dataset is small and synthetic: only 8 scenes (6 train/2 out-of-domain), which makes the 'large-scale' claim questionable and limits the diversity of the out-of-domain test. All quantitative perception results rest on this narrow synthetic distribution; in-the-wild generalization is supported only by qualitative figures in the supplement.

The core 3D-scene contribution is evaluated qualitatively only. There are no metrics for reconstructed geometry quality (e.g., mesh accuracy, multi-view consistency after completion) or for downstream PBR relighting fidelity, even though 'graphics-ready 3D scenes' is the headline claim. The authors themselves admit the reconstructed surfaces are bumpy.

The panorama generation result is mixed: FID on SUN360 (39.4) is notably worse than CubeDiff (25.5), yet the text describes this as 'maintaining competitive performance.' A more careful analysis of when/why the method underperforms is needed.

Limited technical novelty in places: circular padding and circularly-wrapped attention are known techniques; the unified formulation (Eq. 3) is essentially conditioning of a flow-matching model, and the Separate-Adapter is a straightforward combination of token concatenation and per-modality LoRAs. The value is primarily in system integration and the empirical finding that priors transfer.

Engineering-heavy design: 12 separately trained adapter models on a non-open-weight base model (Flux.1-dev, with license restrictions) raises reproducibility concerns; the project page link is incomplete ('available at' with no URL), and no code or dataset release commitment is stated.

Some claims are asserted rather than demonstrated, e.g., 'superior generalization performance' for in-the-wild images with no quantitative comparison, and the motivation that seam artifacts 'fundamentally originate' from lack of circular equivariance is argued informally rather than analyzed.

Writing has minor sloppiness (e.g., 'and and' in Sec. 4.3, 'Roughnes' label in Fig. 8, unfinished project-page sentence), and several key details (task configurations, padding-size choices) are deferred entirely to the supplement.

strengths: Unified and well-motivated framework: repurposing pre-trained 2D flow-matching models (Flux.1-dev) for panorama generation, perception (RGB to distance/normal/albedo/roughness/metallic), and completion within a single formulation (Eq. 3) is an elegant contribution that addresses a real gap — prior panorama-based 2D lifting methods generate appearance but neglect intrinsic PBR properties.

Circular Synchronization is a technically clean, training-free solution to the panorama seam problem: enforcing circular translation equivariance in all spatial operators (circular padding for convolutions; token padding plus attention masking for RoPE-based attention) is better principled than latent-level blending/rotation tricks, and the qualitative comparison in Fig. 10 supports the claim.

The Separate-Adapter (modality-specific LoRA) design is empirically validated against Shared-Branch and Shared-Adapter alternatives (Table 5), and the ablations on pre-trained priors vs. training from scratch convincingly demonstrate the value of 2D generative priors even for modalities with very different statistics.

PanoX fills a genuine dataset gap: the first panorama dataset with dense geometry and material annotations spanning both indoor and outdoor scenes (Table 1), with sensible train/test/out-of-domain splits that enable generalization evaluation.

Broad experimental coverage: quantitative comparisons on panorama generation (Table 2), intrinsic decomposition (Table 3), geometry estimation (Table 4), completion (Table S1), plus supplementary ablations (camera rays, PBR input arrangements, joint distance-normal modeling) that show scientific care — including reporting negative results (Tables S2, S4).
Honest and substantive limitations section covering inference efficiency, bumpy reconstructed surfaces, and poor metallic generalization, which appropriately calibrates the claims.
weaknesses: Table 4 (geometry estimation) contains suspicious and poorly specified numbers: the header defines Mean/Median normal error with a down-arrow but does not state units, baseline values (e.g., DiffusionRenderer Mean 97.19, OmniData-v2 Median 100.60 where Median > Mean) are implausible under a degrees interpretation, and the 5°/30° columns are reported as fractions while baseline values (0.001, 0.023) suggest near-total failure of strong published methods. The fairness of comparing narrow-FoV/depth-only methods on out-of-domain panoramas without adaptation is also questionable, making the claimed 'second highest depth accuracy' hard to verify.

Claims of 'state-of-the-art performance across both' datasets in Table 2 are overstated: CubeDiff beats OmniX on Laval Indoor KID (0.32 vs 0.41) and substantially on SUN360 FID (25.5 vs 39.4). The paper should present these results as mixed rather than uniformly superior.

The strongest application — PBR-ready 3D scene generation — is evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. 11, supplementary videos). There is no quantitative assessment of reconstructed mesh quality, no user study, and no comparison against alternative panorama-to-3D pipelines, so the practical impact of the full system remains undemonstrated beyond demos.

Evaluation of perception relies heavily on the authors' own PanoX-OutDomain split, whose rendering characteristics match PanoX-Train; on the external Structured3D benchmark only albedo is reported. Broader third-party benchmark coverage would strengthen the generalization claims, especially given the acknowledged poor generalization of Pano2Metallic.

The system requires 12 separately trained adapter models (one per task/modality), which increases engineering complexity and training cost; a single multi-task model, or discussion of why this was not pursued, is missing. Inference efficiency inherited from Flux is acknowledged but not quantified (no runtime/latency numbers).

Dependence on Flux.1-dev (a non-commercial-license model) and Florence-2-generated text prompts raises licensing and reproducibility concerns; no code or data release commitment is stated in the manuscript beyond a project-page URL.

Eq. 5 (the MIMO loss) is presented but never used or evaluated in the main paper, and the distinction between it and the per-task training regime actually adopted is left to the supplementary material, creating some ambiguity about the final trained configuration.
